title: Leaks and How to Find Them
summary: A leak is memory nobody frees. Why leaks matter in programs that run for hours, how the MSVC debug heap reports them at exit with an allocation number you can break on, heap snapshots in Visual Studio, AddressSanitizer for leaks and use-after-free, and counting your own allocations.

cards.q: Why is a leak in a long-running game more serious than in a short command-line tool?
cards.a: Windows reclaims everything when a program exits, but a game that leaks a little every frame keeps growing for hours until it slows down or runs out of memory.

cards.q: The leak report shows {157} normal block. How do you find the code that allocated it?
cards.a: Call _CrtSetBreakAlloc(157) at the start of main and run again; the debugger stops when allocation 157 happens.

cards.q: A leaked block's data shows CD CD CD CD. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The block was allocated but never written to.

cards.q: Name two bugs AddressSanitizer reports at the moment they happen.
cards.a: Any of: heap, stack or global buffer overflow, use after free, use after return, double free, mismatched new[]/delete.
